items.title: Farewell to arms?
items.description: PALESTINIAN resistance group Hamas recently made a major concession by agreeing to give up its weapons. It should be remembered that along with its political activities, the movement has an armed wing dedicated to the liberation of Palestine. The group’s weapons will be surrendered to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the Palestinian technocratic body formed under US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. In essence, Hamas has thrown the gauntlet to Israel: it is ready to surrender its weapons, but will the Zionist state end its occupation of Gaza? This remains the million-dollar question. Mr Trump was upbeat about the development, saying that Israel was “very happy” about it. However, while there had been no official reaction from Tel Aviv at the time of writing, most Israeli politicians, including some in the cabinet, have decried the move, calling for the destruction of Hamas. It will be interesting to see whether Israel honours its end of the deal and vacates occupied Palestinian territory in Gaza. Going by past precedent, the Israelis are not known for keeping their word. Also, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces an election in October , and there is widespread anti-Palestinian sentiment amongst the electorate. But the Israeli leader may not want to annoy the American president by appearing to sabotage Mr Trump’s Gaza peace plan. Lest we forget, Israel has murdered over 73,000 Palestinians — more than 21,000 of them children — since the Oct 7, 2023 attacks, and while its killing spree has lessened in intensity, it has not stopped completely since the ceasefire came into effect last year. Moreover, the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains appalling. It should be kept in mind that Hamas and other Palestinian groups have continued their armed struggle against Israel because the Zionist state has closed all avenues of peacefully resolving the Palestine question. Almost the entire Israeli political class is opposed to a Palestinian state, illegal settlements continue to proliferate, and Gaza — which even before the 2023 attacks was virtually under siege — lies in ruins. Meanwhile, Israeli provocations against Al Aqsa have not stopped. If this situation is to change, there must be a clear pathway for a Palestinian state, an end to Israeli brutalities against the Arab population, and complete withdrawal from all occupied territories. Knowing the current political climate in Israel, this is asking for the moon. However, Mr Trump, who sees himself as a ‘peacemaker’, and his BoP must press Israel to at least start the process by withdrawing from Gaza, and allowing unimpeded humanitarian assistance into the Strip. If Tel Aviv does not leave Gaza, it will show the world that it is not serious about peace, and is committed to the occupation of Palestine and to the extermination of the Palestinian people. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

items.title: A hard state?
items.description: THESE days we are repeatedly told that the Pakistani state has been soft on anarchy for far too long. This is the considered and stated position of many state officials as well as of many supporters of those in power. Common people may hold any number of positions that one finds distasteful but the same sentiments being voiced by those in power invite both scrutiny and concern. For the last three years, there has been much chatter about turning Pakistan into a ‘hard state’. No one has given an adequate definition of what this entails, but based on disparate statements and impulses, we can gather this has something to do with protecting the rights of the state and the decision-makers who staff it. These rights are being obtained via a frequently violent trade-off with the rights of the people of Pakistan. The projected consequence of such a trade-off is that protest of all shades becomes a privilege. Demands can only be voiced with due approval through vetted content and NOCs. Speech is to be regulated via defamation, criminalisation laws, and an apparently pliant judiciary till it takes on an acceptable hue, or preferably till it becomes an echo of the state’s. These impulses are neither unique to the Pakistani state nor are they exceptional to this current moment. Trysts with authoritarianism dot the country’s past and arguably lie at the roots of its state structure. British viceregal authority bequeathed an overdeveloped administrative apparatus, which has since then done exceedingly well to reproduce itself and the privileges of those who staff it. When given a chance, politicians of nearly all stripes — centralists, federalists, provincial magnates, or constituency-level bigwigs — have been more than happy to fortify this arrangement for their own and their clients’ benefits. And yet there is a question that should gnaw at anyone who thinks about the trade-off at the table. What is all of this for? If people are being asked to voluntarily or otherwise forfeit their constitutional or social rights, it only makes sense to interrogate what end goal this forfeiture is designed to serve. Beyond the protection of geographic boundaries, what other objectives do limits on individual liberty serve? Forfeiture of individual liberty is commanded by all states in service of some basic objectives. Usually the foremost of these objectives is territorial sanctity: no state tolerates geographic loss and will usually strip people of their rights, property and lives to prevent it. The Pakistani state is fairly typical in this manner. It deals with separatism/secessionism the way many other post-colonial states do, and with variable degrees of success. The bigger question on that front then is whether its strategy for preventing the rise or growth of this factor is useful at all. Beyond the protection of geographic boundaries, what other objectives do limits on individual liberty serve? Other states offer different types of answers. The case of China — paradigmatic for the 21st century — has a very simple one. It places limits on various forms of individual rights for the protection and promotion of the CCP’s endeavours. The main endeavour, since the 1970s at least, has been the growth and collective prosperity of the Chinese people via the unleashing of productive forces (labour and capital), both by the state and by private enterprise. The state under one-party rule decides the degree of this unleashing, its objectives, and ultimately the distribution of its fruits. In the previous century, socialist states decided that the true fulfilment of human life lay in getting rid of privatised forms of exploitation. And so a suspension of individual liberty was done in service of collective ownership of resources, commandeered by the state. Social democratic states in Western Europe decided to infringe on the rights of capital owners over their profit in order to redistribute benefits to the working class via taxation. The late-20th-century Asian Tigers took away social rights of the working poor to generate double-digit capitalist growth. There are other, less palatable answers too. The fascists in Germany stripped the rights, property, and lives of one minority group and various ideological dissenters (primarily the communists) in service of its ethnonationalist and expansionist agenda. At present, the ruling party in India targets individual liberties of specific segments, such as Muslims, to fulfil the cultural agenda of its majority base. In all of these examples, the use of state power is for some larger agenda; a larger agenda in the name of the public (or at least an important part of it), built on specific ideational values and postulates. Something being done in service of something bigger, grander, and to varying degrees, collective. So one must pose the question: what objective does this particular, three-year-old vintage of the ‘hard state’ serve in Pakistan? To date there is no coherent answer. We do not know what the killing of protesters — regardless of the agreeability of their demands — in AJK is going to achieve. What goal banning political movements in the peripheries serves. What Form-47ing election outcomes does. What the hollowing out of the opposition, judiciary, media or civil society helps obtain. If the answer is to maintain territorial integrity, then the vast majority of those whose rights stand stripped away carry no geographic ambitions. If the answer is to unleash GDP growth rates of the kind unseen in the last two decades, then one must reluctantly point out that the needle is yet to move up at all. If the answer is to project sovereignty and stature on the world stage at a time of global upheaval, the logical follow-up is a) whose stature and b) sovereignty in whose name? There are no ready grand answers at the end of this line of inquiry because there is likely no grand thought among those steering the ‘hardening’. The actual answers, if one were to hazard a guess, are probably several degrees more modest: the prolonging of duration in office, an improvement in personal quality of life, and the distribution of gifts and sinecures to a small coterie of loyalists at the expense of everyone else. The writer teaches politics and sociology at Lums. X: @umairjav Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

items.title: Missing weapon, forensic inconsistencies puzzle investigators in Raza ‘murder’ case
items.description: KARACHI: Police investigators probing the death of a 25-year-old former IBA student and aspiring businessman have found that Mir Raza Ali Khan was facing financial losses in his business, but they doubt the theory that he took his own life, even though the evidence collected so far points to suicide, it emerged on Sunday. They are, however, hopeful of “resolving the case within a very short time”. The aspiring businessman’s body, bearing a gunshot wound to his chest, was recovered from bushes near Shahi Qila in Gulistan-i-Jauhar, opposite the University of Karachi, two days after he went missing and was allegedly kidnapped from his home in PECHS, Block-2. One official familiar with the investigation so far told Dawn , on condition of anonymity, that certain things had emerged during the course of the investigation, prompting investigators to focus more on the possibility of suicide than murder. Detectives trace former IBA student and entrepreneur’s final movements; financial losses emerge as key focus in probe Elaborating, the official said that Raza, as usual, arrived at his home in PECHS, early in the morning after closing his shop at Bahadurabad Chowrangi. After some time, he went back to his shop/office, where he took a pistol and returned in his car. He left the keys to his car and house. He also left his watch and some cash for his mother. Inside the home, he deleted all the data from his iPhone. The official added that Raza hired an online cab and asked the driver to play his favourite song, according to the driver’s statement recorded by investigators. He paid the driver double the required fare. CCTV footage from the place where the driver dropped him off in Gulistan-i-Jauhar showed that he was “roaming” around, and no one else was seen accompanying him. After deleting all the data from his phone, he went offline. It has been established that he himself deleted the data. He may have thrown away his mobile phone, which was later picked up by someone from the place where his body was found. When the person inserted a SIM card into the phone, investigators traced and detained him and recovered the deceased’s mobile phone. The holster for the deceased’s pistol was found hanging from a tree along the same route where the body was found. It was possible that, like his mobile phone, the pistol was taken away by someone passing through the area. The officer said the deceased had suffered financial losses amounting to millions of rupees in investments, and he was supposed to return money invested by others. He added that Raza had asked one investor for a Rs30m loan because he was facing financial difficulties, but the request was declined. The alleged investor also told police that the deceased had told him he was having “weird thoughts”. His fiancée, in her statement to police, said that he was “obsessed” with his Bitcoin investment. She also told investigators that she had sent him a message late that night, but since he was already offline, he did not receive it. The officer said that despite all these developments, which strongly suggested the possibility of suicide, investigators still had three doubts. First, why did he travel to and choose that place in Gulistan-i-Jauhar? Secondly, his pistol has not been recovered so far, though the holster has been recovered. Thirdly, doctors told police that the bullet had been fired into his chest from close range. Yet gunshot residue was not detected on his hands, which is normally found when been recovered. Thirdly, doctors told police that the bullet had been fired into his chest from close range. Yet gunshot residue was not detected on his hands, which is normally found when someone takes their own life using a firearm. It was possible that, since the body was partially decomposed, the residue on his hands could no longer be detected. Another officer, who is also familiar with the probe, said that investigators were making sincere and intensive efforts under the supervision of senior police officers. The call record data (CRD) of the deceased, along with details of his family background and friends, was also being obtained. Analysis of the available CCTV footage was also underway. The officer said the investigation would produce the “best results within a very short time”. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

items.title: Damage assessment
items.description: PRESIDENT Donald Trump’s approval rating has hit an all-time low according to the latest Economist/YouGov poll. The survey found 62 per cent of Americans disapprove of the president’s performance while 63pc say the country is headed in the wrong direction. These are Trump’s worst numbers since he returned to the White House last year. The results align with findings of other polls, which show he has fallen out of favour with the majority of Americans. The slide isn’t just about an unpopular war with Iran. Trump’s management of the economy is also driving public discontent. The first 18 months of the mercurial leader’s second term have been defined by disruption at home and abroad. His ‘America First’ unilateralism has meant military strikes on multiple countries and upending of the global trading system. It reflects contempt for international law and other nations’ sovereignty. For a president who promised to end wars, not start them, his record is the opposite. Trump assumed American power could browbeat other countries into compliance at no cost to the US. That was a miscalculation. His overreliance on force also failed to produce the results he wanted. Trump may be extreme in his imperious, unilateralist ways but there is continuity with past US conduct in an important respect. Throughout its history of dealing with other nations, the US has underestimated the power of nationalism and the resistance it would meet in trying to force its will on others. It found that in its interventions in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq, which entangled Washington in unwinnable wars, produced strategic blunders and doomed its military adventures. Today, it is finding that again in the war against Iran. Trump also doesn’t seem to understand that the unipolar world long passed into history. In today’s multipolar world, countries will not so easily bend to Washington’s will. Indeed, the more Trump makes blusterous claims and tweets about how he has the power to get what he wants, the more it exposes his inability to secure his goals. There is no shortage of commentary on Donald Trump’s personality and record. Two of the latest books are worth noting. Regime Change by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan and Betrayed: America didn’t vote for this by Ira Shapiro and Anne Kim. Both cover the first year plus of Trump’s second presidency and deliver stinging indictments of his performance. Betrayed is written by a broad coalition of distinguished bipartisan experts from among former government officials, lawyers, scholars and journalists. They are members of what is called the Common Sense Coalition. They chronicle the damage Trump has done to his country and to America’s standing in the world. This damage assessment is undertaken across multiple areas — economy, foreign policy, democracy and free speech, judiciary, voting system, education and climate. The book’s main point is that Americans did not vote for what Trump is doing and the disorder he is producing. His abuses of power must be stopped and his team members held accountable if America’s crisis is to end. With his approval ratings having plunged Trump’s conduct has hardened global attitudes towards the US. Though brief the chapters are pointed. The one on a weaker America is especially sharp. It argues that Trump has fractured the foundations for global stability. His costly and impetuous military adventures without a strategy or respect for international law and his contempt for traditional allies have endangered US security. The authors describe an unchecked president dragging the country into multiple conflicts with scant regard for the fallout. The attack on Iran, they argue, lays bare the hallmarks of his foreign policy decision making — impulsiveness, prioritising force over diplomacy, failure to take rational decisions based on their likely impact and trashing the concerns of allies. They frame his National Security Strategy as a reversal of eight decades of US foreign policy. This has resulted in ‘America Weaker’ and ‘America Alone’ and drained its soft power. Its international stature has diminished. Trump has alienated virtually all allies who had helped the US maintain global peace. The authors also argue Trump has misused and politicised the military and packed it with yes-men afraid of telling him the truth. In the chapter on the rule of law the writers hold Trump guilty of violating limits on presidential power, threatening the integrity of courts and usurping Congressional powers. Core civil liberties have been threatened. He is seen as weaponising government machinery including the Justice Department to punish political opponents and suppress dissent. He has violated court orders and vilified judges while shielding his friends from legal accountability. Regime Change is no less scathing about Trump’s record in office. Its subtitle Inside the imperial presidency of Donald Trump indicates its focus is on the inner workings of the White House. It is a riveting, richly sourced account of the chaos wreaked by a president who has acted with impunity and radically changed the office he occupies. It narrates how efforts have been made to stop Trump but failed. Based on over 1,000 interviews, it takes the readers behind the scenes to offer insights into Trump’s decision-making that has been so consequential and of course harmful for the country. How his team fell in line with his decisions even when they strongly disagreed is exemplified by a telling exchange between Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu during his February visit to Washington when he convinced Trump to attack Iran. The Israeli leader assured Trump that regime change would succeed in Iran and its nuclear capability would be destroyed, before Tehran could seize the Strait of Hormuz. The CIA director rubbished this view while the secretary of state called it “farcical”. But Trump prevailed. Trump’s conduct has hardened global attitudes toward the US. Friends, allies and adversaries view the erratic swings in American policy with alarm. The latest poll by the Pew Research Centre captures the shift. China is viewed more favourably than the US in most countries surveyed. Given the turbulence of the past 18 months, that result is hardly unexpected. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

items.title: Living with leopards in the Himalayas
items.description: In the afternoon of Feb 22, 67-year-old Bulal Maharjan, a farmer on the outskirts of Kathmandu, was sitting on his porch chopping cauliflower leaves to feed his chickens. Hearing a loud thud as a parked motorcycle toppled, he turned and watched in horror as a leopard leapt away from the fallen vehicle and lunged at him, piercing its sharp canines into his forehead, its claws lacerating his hands. Within seconds, neighbours swarmed in, and the leopard ran into a nearby house. They eventually trapped the animal inside. After nearly two hours of panic that saw two more people injured trying to control the distressed big cat, forest division officials managed to sedate it and bring the situation under control. Maharjan still can’t shake off memories of the attack. “For three days straight, I couldn’t even sleep. Every time I began to doze, the scene of this attack would jolt me up!” he says. “I think we should just get rid of this animal. Period.” Conflicts with people are growing as expanded forest land and climate change push the creatures into human settlements Sentiments like Maharjan’s are common across Nepal, where leopards have been responsible for significant loss of human life and livestock. Research shows that from the years 2000 to 2020, conflicts between humans and four large mammals — elephants, rhinos, tigers and common leopards — claimed 887 human lives and led to the killing of 1,139 animals. Of these, common leopards were the leading cause of human deaths at an average of 19 deaths per year, and the species most frequently killed. To try to bring the conflict under control, Nepal and other countries with human-large predator conflicts are exploring a range of solutions. Nepal has three ecological zones: lowland dominated by Bengal tigers, mountainous regions where snow leopards roam free, and the vast mid-hill ruled by common leopards as the top predator. While protected areas in the lowlands and mountains receive dedicated conservation funding for their charismatic predators, the mid-hills are largely managed as community forests. The celebrated community forest program is a key reason for leopards’ thriving in the mid-hills. In the early 1990s, amid worsening floods and landslides linked to forest degradation, King Birendra handed over management of large swaths of forest to local communities so that they would have stakes in conservation, and benefit from timber and fruit harvests. Today, almost 47 per cent of Nepal is covered by forest patches. About a third of that area belongs to community forests, most of which are run by people living in the mid-hills. “But what the communities didn’t realise was they also restored habitats so that the top carnivores could return,” said Kedar Baral, a wildlife biologist for Nepal’s Bagmati province. In 2020, Baral’s team conducted an analysis of leopard scat collected in the mid-hills that showed that 27pc of the animals’ diet consisted of domestic animals, while the wild ungulates that big cats typically prefer to hunt, like barking deer and wild boars, made up only 10pc. In search of sprouting leaves, barking deer venture from the dense community forests to farmland, and “as the deer enter the farmlands, that’s where the leopard follows,” says Baral, bringing them into contact with domestic livestock. Nepal’s hydropower and construction projects are also expanding into remote forested areas at higher elevations, disturbing habitat and bringing workers as well as a new hunting pressure against top predators, including common leopards, living there. That forces the leopards and their prey to leave their territory, says Madhu Chetri, a wildlife ecologist at the National Trust for Nature Conservation. Climate change might be influencing conflict patterns, too. While he was working as a district forest officer in Nepal’s western mid-hills, Baral and his team were repeatedly called to respond to common leopard attacks on local communities. Over time, he noticed a change in the pattern: Conflict incidents and human or livestock deaths were increasingly reported from higher-elevation settlements. Reporting in 2023, Baral and colleagues investigated whether climate change was driving this shift. Using data from 343 sites across Nepal based on signs of leopard scat, animal tracks and kills, he modeled habitat preferences of leopards, considering factors such as temperature, rainfall and elevation. The results suggest that leopards prefer mid-hill conditions at around 1,000 meters with moderate temperatures and high rainfall. Warming climates are likely expanding the range of suitable habitat uphill, which could allow the leopard population to grow and, as a result, have a higher risk of conflict with humans. Of course, it is a conservation success to be celebrated when numbers of threatened or endangered large carnivores increase — whether they be lynx, wolves, tigers or leopards — but it also presents new challenges, says Philip Nyhus, a conservation biologist at Colby College in Maine. Solutions to the problem have two parts, he adds: first, to keep wildlife separate from people and their livestock to prevent conflict to begin with, and second, to mitigate impacts when conflicts do occur. “A lot of attention has been given to the second piece,” he says. “What would be better is if we could prevent conflict from happening in the first place.” There are international examples to draw from. In the Argentinian Dry Chaco forest, for example, small households in woody areas have faced frequent attacks by pumas on sheep and goats. Sofia Nanni, a conservation biologist at the National Scientific and Technical Research Council of Argentina, worked with locals to come up with the idea of trying spiked leather collars on livestock, an approach that had proved successful in reducing leopard attacks on cows in countries like Iran. “We found a local artisan who made collars for dogs and we asked him if he could make collars,” Nanni says. Tracking collared goats and sheep for two years, her team found that the puma predation in uncollared animal groups was 10 times higher than that in collared groups. Several other strategies are successfully reducing leopard and other top predator conflicts globally. Still, changing attitudes and implementing effective interventions, as well as better compensation, can take years, while frustration among affected communities continues to grow. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

items.description: LONDON: Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has signalled his support for a written Constitution for the UK, which unlike most countries, does not have one authoritative document. Since entering office just two weeks ago, the former mayor of Greater Manchester has made devolution of power to regional authorities a focus of his administration. “In the end, I think it does start to point towards a new constitutional settlement,” Burnham said of his devolution plans. Calling for a “new clear set of principles about how this country should be run”, Burnham said there was a need for a written Constitution – something he has called for before he was prime minister. “It’s wrong that people are left arguing for things that are just fundamental… and the lack of a Constitution disempowers places in that situation,” said Burnham. items.title: Woman bomber kills 3 near Moscow restaurant
items.description: MOSCOW: A homemade bomb carried by a woman killed at least three people and injured 21 near an upscale restaurant in central Moscow on Saturday evening, authorities said, amid unconfirmed speculation on social media that the attack may have been linked to the war in Ukraine. The explosion occurred just before 8pm close to an Italian restaurant located in one of Moscow’s seven Stalin-era skyscrapers at Kudrinskaya Square, the police said. Russia’s National Anti-Terrorism Committee (NAK) said an unidentified woman carrying an improvised explosive device had tried to get into the restaurant but had been stopped by a security guard. NAK said the woman, the guard and a customer at the Balzi Rossi Italian restaurant had been killed instantly in the blast that followed. REN TV cited a source on Sunday as saying that two people who had been taken to hospital had later died of their wounds, bringing the death toll to five, though there was no official confirmation. The channel said six people remained in a serious condition. Reports suggest top Russian commander was intended target, but remained unharmed Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin on Sunday offered his condolences to the families of those killed and said those responsible would be punished. “A brutal terrorist attack was carried out in Moscow yesterday,” he said in a statement. Heavily armed law enforcement officers sealed off the scene of the attack on Saturday. The authorities did not name those killed or injured or any suspects. Unverified social media reports suggested that a top Russian military commander had been the intended target but had been unharmed. More than four years into a full-scale war with Ukraine, Russia this year promised better protection for high-ranking military officials after a series of assassinations and attempted killings, which it blamed on Kyiv. Russian war bloggers, without citing any evidence, were quick to blame Ukraine for the attack. Kyiv did not immediately comment. The Kommersant daily suggested that the woman carrying the bomb may not have known about it, and that it had been set off remotely by someone else. The restaurant’s website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a private event. The nature of the attack recalled a bombing carried out in 2023 that killed Russian pro-war blogger Vladlen Tatarsky. A young woman, Darya Trepova, was jailed for 27 years for delivering a bomb concealed inside a statuette that exploded in Tatarsky’s hands. She said she had been acting under instruction from a man in Ukraine who had sent her money. Senior Ukrainian officials at the time neither claimed responsibility nor denied involvement. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

items.title: US and Japan jointly intervene to prop up yen in rare move
items.description: Japan and the US have confirmed that they jointly intervened last week to halt a slide in the yen after it weakened to a fresh 40-year low. The joint intervention is the first since 2011, when both countries took coordinated action to weaken the yen after the devastating earthquake and tsunami that hit eastern Japan. Both Japan’s finance ministry and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have said that they will not hesitate to conduct joint interventions in the future. It highlights both countries’ efforts to prevent a sell-off in the yen and Japanese government bonds from affecting the global economy, including potentially pushing up borrowing costs for Washington. “The United States agreed to participate in the coordinated intervention because it serves its national interests by offering the prospect of significant benefits at a low cost,” Shigeto Nagai, head of Japan economics at Oxford Economics, told the BBC. The two countries are expected to continue to intervene “intermittently in a coordinated manner for some time”, he added. “Even if the actual amount of intervention is not particularly large, the prolonged sense of vigilance regarding intervention will be effective in deterring speculators.” The yen has historically been weak mainly because Japan has maintained much lower central bank interest rates than other major economies like the US. That makes the Japanese currency less attractive to international investors. The Bank of Japan last raised interest rates in June, as it increased its main rate to 1% – the highest level since September 1995. In comparison, the US Federal Reserve’s benchmark rate is in a range of 3.50% to 3.75%. Japan also faces a decades-long decline in its working-age population, low productivity, and a heavy reliance on energy imports priced in US dollars. On Monday, Japan’s finance ministry said Friday’s intervention with the US Treasury Department “countered excessive volatility and disorderly movements in the Japanese yen in recent months”. The “coordinated foreign exchange actions countered disorderly yen movements,” Bessent said in a social media post. “We strongly support Japan’s decisive market and monetary steps to correct the substantial undervaluation of the yen,” he added. “They have a weakening yen, and they wanted a little bit of help. And we’re always there for Japan,” US President Donald Trump told reporters on Sunday. A notepad photographed in front of US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent on Friday The dollar fell by 0.2% to 157.07 yen after Trump’s comments, well off the 40-year high of 164 last month, but rose back to 157.70 yen after the Japanese finance ministry’s statement. Bank of Japan data indicated that Tokyo may have sold almost $59bn of US dollar to buy yen when it intervened in New York markets on Thursday, before Friday’s confirmed joint intervention with Washington. The US has not confirmed the size of its intervention but a Reuters photograph of a notepad in front of Bessent during a a cabinet meeting on Friday read: “To Do: Buy Japanese Yen $5-10 bil”.

items.title: L'administration Trump approuve des pesticides qui inquiètent la communauté scientifique
items.description: L'approbation récente par le gouvernement américain de plusieurs nouveaux pesticides inquiète scientifiques et associations environnementales, qui estiment que ces substances sont en réalité des PFAS, surnommés polluants éternels, à l'usage de plus en plus restreint en Europe. Les PFAS sont des substances chimiques synthétiques inventées par l'homme, présent des vestes de pluie aux poêles antiadhésives au téflon, jusqu'aux pesticides pour l'agriculture. Mais il existe un débat sur la définition de ce qui constitue un PFAS. Les cinq substances récemment autorisées ne rentrent pas dans la définition des PFAS adoptée par les autorités fédérales américaines. Pour de nombreux experts, ces produits sont pourtant bien des polluants éternels et ils alertent sur la dangerosité de ces nouveaux pesticides pour l'environnement. L'AFP fait le point sur ce débat. Question de classification Les PFAS se caractérisent par leur structure chimique: ils contiennent des liaisons carbone-fluor très stables. Leur résistance à la corrosion, à la lumière ou aux fortes chaleurs en font d'excellent isolants, anti-adhérents ou imperméabilisants. Une définition de ce que constitue un PFAS, basée sur leur structure chimique et adoptée par l'OCDE en 2021, a été suivie par environ la moitié des Etats américain, le Congrès et le Pentagone, de même que par un groupe de 150 scientifiques dans un consensus annoncé en 2024. Mais en 2023, l'Agence américaine de protection de l'environnement (EPA) a choisi sa propre définition, plus restrictive. Sous le mandat de Joe Biden, quand cette définition a été adoptée, un seul pesticide a été approuvé, contre cinq depuis le retour de Donald Trump au pouvoir. L'EPA souligne aujourd'hui que ces pesticides sont autorisés dans d'autres pays et sont indispensables pour la sécurité alimentaire. Partie émergée de l'iceberg Mais pour des scientifiques et des militants environnementaux, les nouvelles substances autorisées en raison de cette classification restrictive présentent tout de même des dangers pour l'homme et l'environnement. Il existe des « preuves qui suggèrent un potentiel cancérigène », a elle-même reconnu l'EPA dans son évaluation d'un des herbicides nouvellement autorisé, le trifludimoxazin. Et ces nouvelles autorisations ne représentent que la partie émergée de l'iceberg: une analyse menée en 2024 sur les substances déjà autorisées aux Etats-Unis et au Canada a conclu que 66 d'entre elles étaient des PFAS, selon la définition de l'OCDE. « C'est un problème qui a été mis sous le tapis par les gouvernements successifs », dénonce Nathan Donley de l'association environnementale Center for Biological Diversity. « Mais ça devient pire aujourd'hui. » Sur dix pêches achetées dans le commerce aux Etats-Unis, « il y a de bonnes chances que neuf aient des résidus de PFAS très toxiques », alerte Varun Subramaniam, qui a mené des analyses pour l'ONG Environmental Working Group. Nombre de ces pesticides se dégradent en TFA, un polluant omniprésent dans l'eau. L'Autorité européenne de sécurité des aliments a durci fin juillet ses recommandations sur les doses admissibles de cette substance extrêmement persistante que l'on retrouve dans les sols, les nappes phréatiques, les cultures agricoles, et in fine, dans l'eau potable et l'alimentation humaine. Lobbyistes Les ONG ont critiqué des liens forts entre l'industrie et les régulateurs américains. Le chef de l'EPA, Lee Zeldin, a fait modifier en novembre la page web sur les PFAS et les pesticides du site de l'agence pour en retirer toute mention d'une plus large définition des polluants éternels, selon des documents publics obtenus par le Center for Biological Diversity. Le même jour, le lobby de l'industrie américaine des pesticides, CropLife America, publiait un argumentaire anti-régulation qui citait la page nouvellement révisée. Le lobby a affirmé à l'AFP qu'il n'y a eu aucune coordination. Un débat qui rappelle à Cindy Hu, une chercheuse en science de l'environnement à l'Université George Washington, des épisodes précédents. Quand la première génération des PFAS a été progressivement retirée au début des années 2000, l'industrie les a remplacés par d'autres molécules vendues comme plus sûres. Mais l'une d'entre-elles a depuis provoqué d'importantes contaminations dans l'eau potable en Caroline du Nord. « C'est une nouvelle version de la même histoire », se désole-t-elle, défendant un principe de précaution selon lequel ces substances chimiques devraient être considérées dangereuses, à moins de la preuve du contraire. The post L'administration Trump approuve des pesticides qui inquiètent la communauté scientifique appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Firefighters under pressure amid raging wildfires
items.description: AGIOS KONSTANTINOS: North America and Europe have been ravaged by wildfires this summer after a period of record-breaking heatwaves and little rain conditions that scientists say have been exacerbated by climate change. In Greece, two firefighting helicopters collided while helping to control a huge wildfire on Sunday that has destroyed more than 100 homes northwest of Athens, while a fresh blaze forced evacuations on the popular tourist island of Kefalonia. State broadcaster ERT reported that one crewmember had been found safe, while rescuers were searching for the second. Television footage showed one of the helicopters explode and plunge to the ground in flames after an apparent rotor collision. Helicopters collide in Greece as tourist destinations evacuated; blazes in Spain, France show signs of easing; flames roar through Spokane as Washington state declares emergency Meanwhile, destructive blazes in France and Spain showed signs of easing over the weekend, but several wildfires have broken out in Greece after a period of relative calm there. Gale-force winds that had fuelled a fire around Porto Germeno on the Gulf of Corinth 60 km (40 miles) northwest of Athens subsided, but flames crossed a mountain to the south and reached the settlement of Veniza and a military firing range, igniting unexploded ordnance. Firefighters focused their efforts on preventing fire from advancing towards the coastal town of Megara, which has a population of around 30,000. In France, wildfires in the Gironde and Var departments showed signs of easing. Authorities reported only minor flare-ups in the southwestern Gironde area and said the blaze in the southeastern Var department had not spread overnight. In Monfort-Sur-Argents, in the region of Var, Georges Blanc, who fled from the fire, returned home and was busy putting out hot embers to prevent a flare-up, while firefighters watered the wider area. In central Spain, wildfires that ripped through tens of thousands of hectares over the past week were mostly under control, though firefighters were dealing with reignitions in some areas. In the western province of Caceres, a forest blaze erupted on Saturday, prompting the evacuation of around 800 people. Those residents were allowed to return on Sunday but remained confined to their homes as the fire was still active. Meanwhile, a fast-moving wildfire roared through the US city of Spokane on Saturday, forcing thousands of residents to evacuate as Washington state declared an emergency over one of its worst fire seasons on record. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson declared a state of emergency and noted that the Pacific Northwest state is enduring a fourth consecutive year of drought as climate change creates conditions propitious for destructive wildfires. Blazes are burning around the region. More than 200,000 acres (80,900 hectares) were burning across the northwestern state during a record fourth consecutive year of statewide drought. Video of the wildfire shot by people driving through the city of some 230,000 on Saturday showed house after house engulfed by flames or reduced to ash as wind-fueled blazes burned out of control in hot, bone-dry weather. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

items.title: New Spider-Man film sees second-best global opening weekend ever
items.description: Spider-Man: Brand New Day brought in $927m (£687m) of global ticket sales to make it the second-biggest opening weekend ever as it shot past its estimated $225m production budget. The superhero movie – starring real-life husband and wife Tom Holland and Zendaya – is only behind Avengers: Endgame , which took in more than $1.2bn in its opening weekend in 2019. Brand New Day also set a second-best North American record, with box office takings of $335m. The film’s strong performance gives a much-needed boost for Disney ahead of the highly-anticipated December release of Avengers: Doomsday , after a string of Marvel movies underperformed in recent years. Brand New Day, which opened in cinemas last week, picks up a few years after 2021’s Spider-Man: No Way Home as Peter Parker continues to fight crime in a world that has forgotten he is the masked superhero. The latest instalment of the hugely popular franchise received largely positive reviews, with some calling it Holland’s best Spider-Man performance yet . The film is Marvel’s last big-screen outing before Doomsday, the long-awaited culmination of multiple superhero story arcs after Avengers: Endgame. Marvel films released since Endgame have struggled to attract the same broad audiences as they did at their peak. Big budget films like The Marvels and The Thunderbolts recouped their production costs but were among the studio’s lowest-grossing films. Spider-Man remains one of Marvel’s most lucrative franchises, with No Way Home making nearly $2bn in ticket sales. Cinema attendance has slowed since the Covid-19 pandemic, which accelerated the shift to home-streaming options like Netflix. But the big screen has staged something of a comeback this year, with the North American box office takings on track to pass $10bn for the first time since 2019. That was helped by blockbuster hits by including Toy Story 5, Michael, and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie – which have made more than $1bn each. July releases Brand New Day and The Odyssey – director Christopher Nolan’s take on the epic Greek poem – are also on track to top the $1bn mark. Indie horror flicks Obsession and Backrooms emerged as surprise successes , bringing in more than $390m each despite their modest budgets.

items.title: Scuffle and chaos mar MQM-P meeting as two groups clash at party's office in Karachi's Bahadurabad
items.description: KARACHI: At least four people were injured as a scuffle and chaos marred a meeting of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) at the party’s headquarters in Bahadurabad near Char Minar on Sunday evening. According to party officials, the clash broke out between supporters of two rival groups within the party. A police officer, requesting anonymity, told Dawn that police were present at the scene and the situation was under control. He added that, so far, no one had approached the New Town police to lodge a complaint. The official added that police contingents had rushed to the scene to prevent the situation from deteriorating further. Another police official told Dawn that at around 7:20pm, an MQM-P meeting was underway at the party’s temporary headquarters in Bahadurabad, where senior leaders were present. He said the situation escalated after Dr Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui left the meeting, with a scuffle breaking out between workers belonging to groups led by Anis Qaimkhani and Mustafa Kamal, and those supporting Dr Siddiqui and Aminul Haque. It was not clear what led to the scuffle between the two groups. According to the official, workers from the Qaimkhani group allegedly assaulted members of the Siddiqui group and forcibly removed them from the party’s headquarters. Later, Siddiqui group workers gathered at a nearby park. The official said heavy firing was also reported from inside the party headquarters, causing fear and panic in the area. One person, identified as Amir Ali, 40, sustained a bullet injury and was shifted to Abbasi Shaheed Hospital. Later, Farooq Sattar, Ali Khursheedi and Haque arrived at the park and asked the workers to come for a press conference, which did not take place, the police officer added. At around 10pm, the leaders left the party headquarters and the workers also dispersed. Police remained present at the site, but no arrests were made, the official added. Meanwhile, police surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed said one person with a firearm injury and three others injured by sticks and stones were brought to Abbasi Shaheed Hospital from Bahadurabad. She added that the person with the firearm injury, who had wounds on his arm and chest, was later shifted to a private hospital. In a post on X, Sindh government spokesperson Sadia Javed said: “They set out to divide Sindh, but failed to keep their own house in order.” “Those who sought to divide others have themselves splintered into factions today. The people have once again given a fitting response to those who pursued the politics of hatred against Sindh’s unity,” Javed said. “Every dream of dividing Sindh was buried before, and it has been buried once again today. Sindh was united, Sindh is united and Sindh will remain united.”

items.title: Malaysian boy to go on trial for allegedly murdering girl in school
items.description: A teenage boy in Malaysia is set to go on trial on Monday for allegedly killing a female schoolmate, in a high-profile case that has sparked debate about the effects of social media on children. The boy is accused of murdering 16-year-old Yap Shing Xuen last October. The girl was found fatally stabbed multiple times in a toilet at their secondary school on the outskirts of the capital Kuala Lumpur. The boy, who was 14 at the time, has pleaded not guilty. If convicted, he could spend decades in prison. Police previously said they suspected social media could have influenced the boy. Police also confirmed a note was found on him at the time of his arrest. Reports about the note’s alleged content have fueled the wider discussion about the role of social media. Under Malaysian law, the boy cannot be publicly identified as he is still a minor. His young age also means he will not face the death penalty if found guilty. However, he could still face 30 to 40 years in jail, and he could also be flogged. The age of criminal responsibility in Malaysia is 10 years old. The case has profoundly shocked the country and triggered a nationwide conversation about the negative effects of social media on children, particularly exposure to the manosphere and incel culture. Some have compared the case to the Netflix series Adolescence, which explores similar themes involving teenage boys, online radicalisation and violence. Last year Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was asked about the case as well as other recent cases of violence in schools. He was quoted by local media as saying that “almost all of these issues stem from the use of mobile phones and social media”, and vowed to look into stricter measures. Authorities have since put in place new rules which they say will protect children and reduce their exposure to harmful online content. Since June, Malaysia has banned all children under the age of 16 from having accounts on major social media platforms.

items.title: Move to create over 100 new additional assistant commissioner posts in Punjab opposed
items.description: LAHORE: The Provincial Manage­ment Service (PMS) officers’ association has opposed the Punjab government’s decision to create 101 Additional Assistant Commissioner (AAC) posts, calling it a “mala fide move” aimed at “weakening” the PMS cadre. The association said the AAC posts were abolished decades ago and their revival was “unnecessary and unjustified”, especially after the establishment of the Punjab Enforcement and Regulatory Authority (PERA) force. The association’s executive committee meeting chaired by president Qamar Zaman Qaisrani decided that an association delegation would meet the Punjab services secretary and the additional chief secretary to explain its concerns and demands on Monday (today). “If PMSA concerns are not addressed, it will launch the first phase of protest by wearing black armbands across the province from Tuesday (tomorrow).” The association said that creating new posts would place an additional burden on the national exchequer and be seen as a direct attempt to undermine the PMS service structure. PMS officers announce protest, say decision ‘undermines’ their service structure Calculating the cost of an AAC and all 101 AACs, the association claims that one such officer would cost the government some Rs46.825 million and all 101 AACs some Rs4.729 billion at once, followed by monthly salaries and privileges. Besides salaries, the cost includes an official vehicle, supporting staff salaries, monthly budgets as well as an office building. The association also expressed serious concerns over alleged discrimination in postings and transfers, delays in promotion boards, and the appointment of junior officers to senior positions. Former administrative secretary Yawar Mehdi commented that the objective of creating AAC posts to improve public service delivery was commendable, provided these officers were empowered to deliver efficient, transparent, and citizen-centric services. However, he added that strengthening field administration should not come at the cost of weakening the civil secretariat or limiting the career progression of PMS officers. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

items.title: Labour in a changing world
items.description: “The times, they are a-changin,” is a 1964 iconic song by legendary Bob Dylan. Times have even changed and evolved in the world of work, even in the Pakistani industrial relations ecosystem. Gone are the days when ego-centric labour leaders wielded influence on members, energising them with demagoguery and rabble-rousing. Gone are the days when they would exert their self-generated importance to browbeat and intimidate employers. Within a few years, they faded away in the sunset. They rarely developed their successors. Narcissism prevailed over pragmatism. A new cadre of labour leaders gradually came to the fore, but by that time the worker movement had lost steam, and the number of labour unions across the country had substantially declined; today, only about one per cent of enterprises have registered unions. This new cadre faced, and is still facing, a difficult task in motivating workers to form unions and display brotherhood. They are reasonably successful in stimulating unions in the public sector but have to move boulders, cross turbulent seas, and remove bottlenecks to achieve entry into targeted individual enterprises. The Pakistan United Workers Federation was formed through the merger of ten moderate labour federations. PUWF is the largest and represents over one million workers in 637 unions. The next large federations are the National Labour Federation and the Pakistan Central Mines Workers Federation. However, most workers’ federations lack the critical mass to build a movement to register unions and have their voices heard in the corridors of power. Although major political parties do have their wings or bureaus, the latter seldom have a formidable say in the parties’ policies. There are labour leaders who are still in a time warp. Their speeches revolve around three or four issues that are ignored by employers and, to some extent, by the government. Their favourite is the issuance of appointment letters for workers because, in their opinion, an appointment letter guarantees job security, even though any worker who is underperforming, displays signs of hostility, or is a chronic absentee will soon be chucked out. Even if that worker knocks at the portals of the courts and even if reinstated, that worker will undoubtedly face resistance from management. Another beef against employers, and this is a genuine complaint, is that the prescribed minimum wage is not given to most of the workers. The minimum wage for unskilled workers provides an essential floor of protection, helps prevent exploitation, and supports the welfare of vulnerable workers. The difficulty for employers arises when the Minimum Wage Board sets wages for semi-skilled and skilled workers, since it may not be in the broader interest of industry and labour market dynamics. Skills, productivity, experience, specialisation, market demand, and sectoral requirements generally determine wages of semi-skilled and skilled workers. Such wages are more appropriately regulated through market mechanisms, collective bargaining, and enterprise-level arrangements. In the majority of countries, a single minimum wage is announced by the government, which ensures that it is paid to every worker. It is standard practice and an accepted norm that the employer determines the wages of skilled employees. A skilled worker will not accept minimum wage unless in dire circumstances. Then there is the mantra of what labour leaders refer to as contract workers. This system is more aptly known as outsourcing of manpower or business functions or third-party employment. It is an employment arrangement in which workers perform services for a principal employer but are formally employed by another entity, such as a contractor, service provider, or outsourcing company. Third-party employment is widely used in both the private and public sectors, particularly for labour-intensive functions or those requiring staffing flexibility. They prefer third-party employment for specific reasons, such as operational flexibility, cost efficiency, specialised expertise, business focus, risk management, and project-based employment. Although there is no bar to outsourcing, this system cannot and should not be used as a means to circumvent existing labour laws. Labour leaders agitate over this issue because such workers cannot join the enterprise union, as they are technically employees of the service provider. On the other extreme, some labour leaders possess a negative attitude and are instrumental in promoting and enriching themselves by disseminating complaints against local enterprises, especially garment and knitwear units, to their foreign associates. These foreign entities, usually radical activists, pump up these complaints by sending them to brands that import from Pakistan and strongly demanding that they cease business with that unit. Although it is much ado about nothing, it impacts the nation’s image as well as exports. The world has changed dramatically over the last few decades, and this transformation is a result of increasing globalisation of business, the growth of multinational corporations, the climate crisis, privatisation, and the rapid pace of technological change. Workers must join hands with employers and agitate for the rationalisation of heavy taxation measures, vociferously condemn and denounce the increase in blatant extortion demands on businesses by extremists and criminals, and influence the government to introduce favourable policies to spur industrialisation. Bob Dylan’s message must be absorbed by labour leaders who are still trapped in a time warp. The lyrics are captivating: “Admit that the waters / Around you have grown / And accept it that soon / If your time to you is worth savin’ / And you better start swimmin’ / Or you’ll sink like a stone / For the times they are a-changin’. The writer is the president of the Employers Federation of Pakistan Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, August 3rd, 2026

items.title: Rethinking our wheat policy
items.description: Pakistan is set to import one million tonnes of wheat as the federal government finds strategic reserves insufficient to meet the provinces’ requirements. More surprisingly, Punjab — the country’s only wheat-surplus province — has also sought 1m tonnes. Wheat imports are not unusual for Pakistan. The country has imported wheat in several financial years over the past decade to bridge supply gaps or rebuild strategic reserves. What makes the current decision unprecedented, however, is its timing. It comes barely three months after harvest, despite repeated official claims, made until only a few weeks ago, that 29.8m tonnes of domestic production, along with over 2m tonnes of carryover stocks, would be sufficient to meet the country’s annual requirements. Adding to the puzzle, poultry feed mills are not consuming wheat this year because maize — the poultry sector’s preferred feed grain — is considerably cheaper. Moreover, the border with Afghanistan has remained closed to both formal exports and cross-border smuggling. Yet wheat prices have surged from around Rs3,300 to Rs4,700 per 40 kg since harvest — well above the import parity price. It reflects a significant supply-demand imbalance. All these developments raise serious questions about the credibility of official wheat production estimates, adequacy of strategic reserves, and the overall management of Pakistan’s wheat supply chain. The proposed 1m tonne import has revived farmers’ fears of a repeat of FY24, when imports triggered a price collapse The core issue is that, while complying with international financial institutions’ conditions, Pakistan’s federal and provincial governments pursued a wheat policy that failed to balance the interests of farmers, who produce the crop, and consumers, who seek affordable flour. They abandoned the decades-old public procurement system without first establishing a credible market-based alternative that could ensure fair returns for farmers, market stability, and adequate strategic reserves. Since Punjab province produces 77 per cent of Pakistan’s wheat, its wheat policy largely shapes the country’s wheat supply chain. Over the last three crops, it adopted three different policies: in 2024, it abruptly stopped wheat procurement from farmers; in 2025, it introduced the Electronic Warehouse Receipt system; and in 2026, it shifted to a private sector-led procurement model by engaging 11 companies. However, none of these delivered the desired results. Meanwhile, despite claiming wheat market deregulation, the Punjab government increasingly relied on administrative interventions — district-specific prices, artificial price caps, raids on stocks held by farmers and private stockists, and restrictions on wheat movement during 2025 and 2026. These measures, aimed at keeping wheat flour affordable for urban consumers, may have temporarily contained prices, but they did so at the expense of farmers by distorting market incentives. The question now is: why has this supply-demand mismatch emerged barely three months after harvest? The answer partly lies in the lower yields and changing behaviour of market participants. After recurring financial losses, farmers cut back on costly phosphate fertilisers. Moreover, heat waves and crop lodging at the maturity stage adversely affected the crop. Consequently, yields declined by an estimated three to five maunds per acre compared with the previous year’s crop. Similarly, on the supply side, learning from last year’s experience, many farmers who could meet their immediate financial needs chose to retain part of their wheat stocks. While individual holdings may be small, the cumulative effect of millions of farmers retaining just a few bags extra translates into millions of tonnes. Likewise, a large number of urban consumers, who usually purchase wheat for a few months’ consumption during harvest, appear to have stocked more this year. Concerns over the Iran conflict, rising world energy prices, and disruptions in global fertiliser supplies fuelled fears of global food inflation. Another important market development has been the growing presence of private stockists in agricultural commodity markets as investors have diverted capital from manufacturing, services, and real estate toward commodity trading. Unlike most farmers, these investors — many of them politically well-connected — have the financial capacity to hold stocks for extended periods. Together, these market dynamics have reduced market supplies and tightened wheat availability. Against this broader backdrop, the central question is: what should Pakistan’s wheat policy be for the next crop? Farmers, already on the verge of financial collapse, are demanding only a harvest-time price at least equal to import parity to offset soaring costs of diesel, electricity, fertilisers, and pesticides. Balancing this legitimate demand while safeguarding consumers’ interests calls for a fundamental rethink of wheat policy. The following three reforms are proposed as a starting point for a broader national debate. First, instead of announcing a support or indicative price, the government should allow unrestricted wheat exports during the harvest time while removing inter-provincial movement restrictions. This would automatically align domestic prices with international markets. Once this happens, exports would naturally become financially unviable for exporters. Second, the government should build and maintain strategic wheat reserves of at least 4m tonnes. These must be procured and released at prevailing market prices rather than under the current practice of administratively fixed rates. These reserves should serve as a market stabilisation tool, released whenever domestic prices rise above import parity levels. If international prices rise sharply, low-income households should be protected through targeted subsidies instead of suppressing farmers’ prices. Third, in a deregulated market, the government should recognise the legitimate role of private stockists — as in the rice and maize markets — rather than branding them as hoarders. By absorbing surplus wheat during harvest, they perform an essential supply-chain function and provide farmers with an alternative marketing channel that reduces the risk of exploitation. However, the government should promote a broad-based network of stockists to prevent excessive market concentration. In conclusion, the proposed 1m-tonne import has revived farmers’ fears of a repeat of FY24, when imports of 3.59m tonnes triggered a collapse in wheat prices. It is high time to formulate a wheat policy through public debate and consensus among all stakeholders, rather than allowing the whims of a few to shape decisions that create opportunities for vested interests and ultimately harm both farmers and consumers. Khalid Wattoo is a development professional and a farmer. Dr Waqar Ahmad is a former Associate Professor at the University of Agriculture, Faisalabad. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, August 3rd, 2026

items.title: Balochistan govt orders inquiry into Sorange coal mine disaster
items.description: • Balochistan Chief Minister’s Inspection Team tasked with determining causes, fixing responsibility for negligence • Four mines sealed as separate departmental inquiry launched QUETTA: The Balochistan government has ordered a high-level inquiry into the deadly coal mine disaster in Sorange that claimed the lives of 34 miners, assigning the investigation to the Chief Minister’s Inspection Team (CMIT) to determine the causes of the tragedy and identify those responsible. On the directives of Balochistan Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti, the CMIT, headed by its chairman Bashir Ahmed Bangulzai, will conduct an on-site investigation into the July 30 accident. The inquiry has been tasked with establishing the actual cause of the incident, reviewing the performance of the relevant authorities, fixing responsibility for any negligence, and proposing measures to prevent similar accidents in the future. According to an official notification issued on Sunday, the CMIT has been directed to submit its findings and recommendations to the chief minister within two weeks. Mines sealed Separately, the mines and minerals department has also initiated a departmental inquiry into the incident. Authorities have sealed four coal mines, including the two directly affected by the accident, as part of the ongoing investigation. The Sorange mine disaster, one of the deadliest mining accidents in Balochistan in recent years, claimed the lives of 34 miners after they were trapped 3,000 to 4,000 feet deep inside the coal mine. Balochistan Chief Inspector of Mines Muhammad Atif said all 34 coal miners hailed from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Shangla district. Abid Yaar, president of the Shangla Coal Mine Workers Association, said Mian Kalay in Shangla’s Pirabad town, from where 23 of the miners hailed, had become an epicentre of repeated coal mine tragedies. He added that the victims, aged between 17 and 25, belonged to the same families and were cousins or close relatives. According to Mr Yaar, several of the deceased were orphans whose fathers had also lost their lives in previous coal mine accidents. The tragedy has renewed concerns over mine safety standards, regulatory oversight and enforcement of safety protocols in the province’s coal mining sector. Officials said the findings of the investigations would help determine accountability and guide future reforms aimed at improving worker safety and preventing similar tragedies. Deadly mine explosions are common in Balochistan, with stakeholders often pointing out the abse­nce of essential safety protocols. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

items.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak is second-largest on record, latest data shows
items.description: Democratic Republic of Congo’s fast-spreading Ebola outbreak is now the world’s second-largest on ‌record, government data showed on Friday, as transmission continues to outpace efforts to contain the epidemic. The number of cases reported across Congo has risen to 3,532, the Communications Ministry said in a statement, with 1,556 deaths recorded. “It’s the fastest-spreading Ebola epidemic that we have ​ever seen,” Carl Skau, acting head of the U.N. World Food Programme, told Reuters this week. “The ​world needs to pay much more attention.” Less than three months since the outbreak began, the ⁠disease has killed five times as many people as previous outbreaks had by the same stage, according to ​Africa’s top public health agency, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo ​strain of the Ebola virus, which has no approved vaccine or treatment. Health responders are also battling insecurity and across eastern Congo, where dozens of armed groups operate, while deep foreign aid cuts have stretched resources. The latest figures about the outbreak ​indicate that only West Africa’s 2014 to 2016 outbreak was bigger, with 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths recorded across ​Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to the World Health Organization. WHO SAYS OUTBREAK MAY BE BIGGER THAN REPORTED Angele Gapio, head of ‌emergencies for ⁠the Caritas charity in the northeastern city of Bunia, said awareness campaigns were failing and frontline responders were exhausted and traumatised. “The disease has now settled in the community,” she told Reuters. “People continue to seek treatment from traditional healers, and the chain of transmission continues.” The WHO said earlier this month the true scale of the outbreak could be ​up to four times higher ​than official figures suggest. Reuters ⁠reported this week that surveillance efforts are stretched due to shortages of vehicles, understaffing and community mistrust. MORE FUNDS NEEDED TO CONTAIN EPIDEMIC Africa CDC said in June it would ​require $1.4 billion to contain the Ebola outbreak, three times its earlier estimate. Figures presented this ​week by Africa ⁠CDC and the WHO showed Congo’s May-August response plan had secured $213.9 million in declared funding, short of planned spending of $242.4 million. A U.S. travel ban is also restricting the supply of aid workers. The Trump administration said earlier this month it ⁠was blocking American ​citizens in Congo from travelling to the U.S. on commercial flights. Samaritan’s ​Purse, which operates treatment centres and relies on U.S. responders for its mission in Congo, said it will have to scale back because of the ​quarantine order.

items.title: Agriculture: Water’s cycle of debt and poverty
items.description: Pakistan today faces a double-barreled water emergency: first, the drying up of surface storage; and second, the relentless depletion of groundwater resources. The country is frequently cited as facing severe water stress, with an estimated storage capacity of only about 30 days compared with an international benchmark of 120 days. In March 2025, Tarbela and Mangla reservoirs fell to or near dead level, and Sindh faced about a 50 per cent water shortage at the start of the kharif season; the Indus River System Authority described depletion to dead levels as a common or usual occurrence in that season. Geopolitical treaty tussles aside, a major challenge in Pakistan’s water sector is that within its own borders, institutional paralysis, siltation of the dams, and huge losses in conveyance are sucking the country’s freshwater into the sea. Nasa’s Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment identifies the Indus Basin as one of the world’s most stressed aquifers, and the rate of depletion is fast, particularly in central Punjab, due to unchecked extraction, climate stress, and failure of regulatory bodies. Pakistan’s vanishing water buffer has resulted in storage gaps and aquifer depletion that impacts small farm holders the most The impact is overwhelming. Driving aquifer depletion places smallholders in a cycle of debt and poverty, and their forced dependence on heavily polluted groundwater leads to chronic illness, child mortality, and the erosion of human capital. Agriculture, which contributes almost 24pc to Pakistan’s GDP and employs more than one-third of the workforce, is the primary driver of water stress, fueled by inefficient canal networks and over 1.3 million unregulated tube wells. Pakistan’s agricultural economy is based on suboptimal and unregulated pumping, which is leading to unsustainable aquifer depletion and aggravating the country’s critical storage problem, making it uncompetitive in the international market. The Pakistan Institute of Development Economics’ research shows that the industry’s demand for water rose by 20pc in the past decade, particularly in the textile, tannery, chemical, and cement sectors. Over 90pc of the industrial plants in Punjab and Sindh operate without regulation, accelerating the rate of groundwater depletion and saline intrusion into important freshwater aquifers. The qualitative deterioration of the country’s water supply is severe, as only a small proportion of wastewater is recycled, and industrial hubs such as Karachi, Faisalabad, and Lahore dump raw chemicals, dyes, and toxic waste into water bodies, thereby constantly polluting domestic groundwater. Without treatment, these toxins can percolate down into the underlying aquifer and directly contaminate the drinking water source for millions of people. The domestic sector accounts for only 4–5pc of total freshwater withdrawals, yet some cities face water shortages; however, governance failures and uncontrolled aquifer mining have direct impacts on municipal access. Consequently, women and young girls suffer from water poverty, spending countless hours walking long distances in rural and peri-urban areas, giving up education, health, and economic independence. The lack of trust and water disputes between provinces undermine national cohesion. Trust among the provinces in the Indus Basin has been fractured by disputed formulas for sharing scarce water and unreliable telemetry data. The reduction in freshwater availability due to climate stress is causing ecological collapse downstream of Kotri, with effects on agricultural GDP, industrial development, and national cohesion, leading to bitter political conflict with the upstream provinces. Stronger provincial environmental protection agencies, backed by strong political will, with clear timelines and dedicated funding, are also critical components of a stronger national and provincial water framework to address policy gaps related to weak targets, neglected water quality, and poor integration with the Sustainable Development Goals. Pakistan also has a plethora of policy documents, such as the National Water Policy (2018) and the provincial water policies (the Punjab Water Act 2019 and the Balochistan Groundwater Ordinance), which provide clear guidelines on water storage, groundwater regulation, and efficient irrigation. However, performance remains poor. If a water security task force is unable to carry out six key imperatives — increasing storage capacity, improving efficiency, managing groundwater, implementing digital telemetry, strengthening climate resilience, and centralising national funding — these policies are unlikely to deliver results. Sustained investment and planning have resulted in higher levels of reserves in other countries, such as Australia (600 days) and Morocco (700 days); Pakistan remains constrained by decades of underinvestment in storage, irrigation modernisation, and wastewater treatment infrastructure. To solve Pakistan’s water problem, there is a need for comprehensive reforms to groundwater recharge, the efficiency of water storage systems, and strong water management policies. The solution to Pakistan’s water crisis requires a combination of policy instruments, such as volumetric pricing of groundwater, non-compliance fines for auditing water-consuming sectors, and subsidised adoption of drip irrigation, and water infrastructure investments, such as small delay-action dams and co-financed industrial effluent treatment plants. Strategic public–private partnerships among industry, donors, and civil society are also critical to rapidly scaling up the use of high-efficiency water technologies. Extensive water depletion and mismanagement not only deplete Pakistan’s aquifers but also cause the loss of flood runoff. Aquifer recharge must be achieved on a large scale. In the short term, farming efficiency has to be improved and surface storage enhanced to secure the nation’s water future. Water is life, but unchecked abstraction and inadequate storage are a direct threat to Pakistan’s survival. However, with good governance, judicious investment and political will, Pakistan can still ensure its hydrological future—because the cost of inaction outweighs the cost of reform. Dr Abida Naurin is an assistant professor and member of Macro Policy Lab at Pide. X: @abida_15 , email: abida@pide.org.pk . Muhammad Mohsin Elahi is an intern at Macro Policy Lab. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, August 3rd, 2026
